source.title: Understanding Pre-training and Fine-tuning from Loss Landscape Perspectives
source.authors: Huan-Ran Chen; Yin-Peng Dong; Ze-Ming Wei; Yao Huang; Yi-Chi Zhang; Hang Su; Jun Zhu

record.file_problem: The supplied metadata title differs from the title in the full text, which is “Unveiling the Basin-Like Loss Landscape in Large Language Models.” The text otherwise appears to be a complete paper.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates safety-task performance under fine-tuning directions and parameter perturbations, but uses loss-landscape and benchmark measures rather than directly measuring refusal rates as in the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure token-position KL, prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, or safety-localized weights. Relevant fine-tuning outcomes are presented mainly as loss-landscape figures; the authors also describe a safety-preserving parameter-noise case. Cited findings from other work were not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the study scores AdvBench safety along SFT directions from adversarial AdvBench fine-tuning (following Qi et al.), Alpaca fine-tuning and a distribution-matched checkpoint. That bears on V1 and V2 by a different method: a 0-1 benchmark landscape along a rescaled direction, not refusal rates of the fine-tuned endpoint. The evidence is figure-only plus the authors' wording.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that LLM loss landscapes on 0-1 benchmarks form basins that widen with scale. Fine-tuning that stays in the basin (their 'benign', distribution-matched sense) preserves capabilities, while adversarial fine-tuning follows near-worst-case directions and degrades them fast. Basin size bounds degradation via randomized smoothing, and the GO optimizer enlarges basins to reduce forgetting. The paper presents this as a loss-landscape explanation of alignment brittleness, not a first-token account.
record.recipe_differences: It studies safety degradation under fine-tuning, including an adversarial dataset setup following prior work, but reports benchmark loss landscapes and basin widths rather than direct harmful-compliance rates. It does not test the token-position KL or bypass methods in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The safety landscape varies with fine-tuning dataset and direction: benign, distribution-shifted Alpaca, adversarial AdvBench, and insecure versus secure code directions.

fits_no_version.finding: Along the insecure-code gradient direction the AdvBench safety basin is much narrower than along the secure-code direction, while MMLU basins are similar.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow insecure-code fine-tuning directions selectively shrink the safety basin without shrinking capability basins (Qwen2.5-7B).

fits_no_version.finding: Under Gaussian parameter noise (σ=0.01), the original and all 9 perturbed Qwen2.5-7B instances refused one AdvBench prompt, with safety score 0.0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random parameter noise within the basin preserves refusal on harmful prompts.

record.problems: The main safety results use benchmark landscapes or basin-width comparisons rather than direct compliance/refusal rates. Several plotted outcomes have no extracted numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The paper notes that its pre-training experiments are limited to NanoGPT scale.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out.

untested.parts: Harmful-compliance or refusal rates. Range of harmful-example counts. Models other than Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Safety of the actual fine-tuned endpoint as opposed to the extrapolated direction.
Safety outcome after ordinary benign fine-tuning such as Alpaca (not stated). Carefully chosen benign data. Refusal rates.
Not tested. The 'Sure, here is' observation is anecdotal; no per-token KL is reported.
Not tested empirically. There is only a heuristic token-substitution bound.
Not tested. The GO optimizer targets basin width at NanoGPT scale, with no safety evaluation.

missing.what: Fine-tuning distances relative to the basin (σ=3e-3, ~251 norm). Alpaca lr=1e-5 is at 3.14 and lr=3e-6 at 0.25; AdvBench lr=1e-6 at 0.071; Qwen2.5-7B-1M at 152.06. The authors say all lie within the basin. This bears on whether the plotted safety collapse occurs at the actual endpoints.

record.verdict_notes: The SFT-case plots rescale the fine-tuning direction to the Gaussian norm. Plotted α values (e.g. ±3e-4 × sqrt(d)) may lie well beyond actual endpoints, so they show sensitivity along a direction rather than the fine-tuned model's safety. The authors' 'benign' differs from Qi et al.'s benign (they call Alpaca 'normal'). The paper cites Qi et al.'s rates (5.5%→31.8%, 1.8%→88.8%); these are cited results, not its own. All fine-tuning results are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct only. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: It does not report harmful-compliance or refusal percentages, or compare a range of harmful-example counts. Its own fine-tuning safety results use benchmark landscapes and an insecure-code fine-tuning direction.
It does not report user-facing harmful-compliance or refusal rates after benign fine-tuning. It evaluates benchmark landscapes for selected fine-tuning directions.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No direct test of compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether training data or objectives produce first-token shallowness.
No training intervention intended to deepen safety across response tokens.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct)
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the adversarial AdvBench dataset for 10 steps; evaluated along the SFT direction.

conditions.value: AdvBench safety benchmark along the SFT direction

rows.measure: Safety benchmark performance / normalized safety loss landscape
rows.value: figure only; text says safety guardrails collapse rapidly along this direction
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe rapid safety collapse, but provide no numerical harmful-compliance or refusal rate here. Other capability benchmarks are described as remaining intact.
rows.check: The authors state that safety guardrails 'collapse rapidly' and the model learns to open with 'Sure, here is'. That is the full V1 effect in direction, so observed rather than partial, though figure-only. The plotted α range is a rescaled direction and may extend beyond the actual 10-step endpoint (Table 3 gives AdvBench distance 0.071).

AdvBench safety benchmark along the benign SFT direction

rows.measure: Safety benchmark performance / normalized safety loss landscape
rows.value: figure only; text says safety is preserved within the most-case basin
rows.note: The reported result is preservation of safety within the basin, not an increase in harmful compliance; no endpoint refusal rate is given.
rows.check: The SFT 'direction' is the official Qwen2.5-7B-1M checkpoint minus the Instruct model, not a user fine-tune on ordinary data. The authors call it 'benign' in their own sense (distribution-matched). Table 3 places it at distance 152 within the basin, so safety is preserved.

relationships.condition: Distribution-matched update (Qwen2.5-7B-1M checkpoint vs Instruct), AdvBench safety
